name: Programming Education
description: Documented Iranian university teaching connects programming languages with software design, debugging, and practical projects. Public materials from Sharif University of Technology and curriculum documentation associated with Ferdowsi University of Mashhad illustrate different approaches, without establishing a nationally uniform learning experience.

seo.title: Programming Education in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented examples of programming education in Iran, including Java, C++, software design, debugging, and university projects.

content.heading: Learning to build software
content.content:
Public teaching materials provide a concrete view of programming education in Iran: students encounter programming languages alongside the tools and design decisions needed to build larger applications. Sharif University of Technology’s Advanced Programming teaching site presents Java, object-oriented programming, graphical interfaces, networking, design patterns, and concurrent programming. Its materials combine explanations, exercises, and project work. This is evidence of a particular teaching approach, rather than a description of every Iranian computing degree. [s1]

Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that combine information with operations. The Ferdowsi University of Mashhad computer-science curriculum documentation places this approach within an advanced programming course that follows introductory programming. Its outline includes functions, recursion, arrays, object relationships, inheritance, exception handling, files, and dynamic memory. The distinction matters: learning another language is only part of the course; students are also expected to reason about program structure and behavior. [s2]

content.heading: Languages, tools, and teaching choices
content.content:
The Mashhad documentation recommends coordinating C++ and Java across advanced programming and data structures, so that students encounter both languages. Where C++ is used, the outline includes modern features such as templates, containers, lambda expressions, and smart pointers. This is a curriculum recommendation, not proof that each instructor follows an identical syllabus. [s2]

Sharif’s public teaching site gives substantial attention to working practices: debugging with an integrated development environment, documenting code, using Git and GitHub, and structuring an application with the Model–View–Controller design pattern. That pattern separates information, presentation, and interaction logic. Project materials also introduce unit testing and code coverage. Together, these elements show how a course can move from isolated answers toward software that students can inspect, revise, and extend. The site is an older teaching resource; its availability does not establish a current enrollment offer or guarantee that every linked dependency still works. [s1]

content.heading: A student project as a teaching example
content.content:
A public student repository identifying itself with Sharif’s Advanced Programming course describes an incremental Java game project. Its authors outline a progression from terminal commands and core game logic to expanded mechanics, graphics, and integration. They identify teamwork, version control, testing, and maintainable architecture as learning goals. [s3]

This example makes the educational process visible: a larger assignment can require students to revisit earlier design decisions as features accumulate. However, the repository is a student-authored account. It does not independently establish assessment results, completion by the whole class, or employment outcomes. Read alongside the course and curriculum pages, it offers a useful illustration of programming practice while leaving the national scale and distribution of such opportunities unresolved. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Artificial Intelligence Education
description: Inspected Iranian teaching materials present artificial intelligence through search, reasoning, probability, and machine learning. Examples from Sharif University of Technology and Mashhad curriculum documentation show that the subject extends beyond using generative applications.

seo.title: Artificial Intelligence Education in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand documented AI teaching in Iran, from search and reasoning to machine learning, mathematical preparation, and public course materials.

content.heading: A subject broader than generative tools
content.content:
The artificial-intelligence course published by Sharif University of Technology introduces intelligent agents through search, knowledge representation, inference, and machine learning. An agent is a system that selects actions in pursuit of an objective; this framing connects different techniques rather than treating artificial intelligence as a single application. The stated learning goals include developing solutions and understanding how methods work well enough to adapt them to particular problems. These are instructional objectives, not independently measured learning outcomes. [s1]

The computer-science curriculum documentation associated with Ferdowsi University of Mashhad provides another example. Its undergraduate AI outline moves from state-space search and constraint satisfaction to adversarial search, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian networks. These topics concern different problems: finding a route through possible decisions, satisfying rules, learning through rewards, or reasoning under uncertainty. Their inclusion demonstrates a broader academic scope than learning to operate a chatbot. [s2]

content.heading: Programming and mathematical preparation
content.content:
Sharif’s published prerequisites include Python programming, data structures, and algorithms, with probability, statistics, and linear algebra strongly recommended. This combination links implementation with mathematical reasoning: students need to express a method in code and understand the assumptions behind it. The page does not present introductory AI as a substitute for these foundations. [s1]

The Mashhad outline instead explicitly lists foundations of logic and algorithm design and analysis as prerequisites. Its syllabus includes uninformed and informed search, the A-star search algorithm, game-tree reasoning, and reinforcement-learning methods. It also covers Bayesian-network representation and inference, including exact methods and approximation by sampling. These differences are useful evidence of how curriculum documents organize preparation; they should not be interpreted as a ranking of institutions or proof of uniform classroom delivery. [s2]

content.heading: What public teaching resources reveal
content.content:
A separate Sharif machine-learning course repository makes slides, Jupyter notebooks, and exercises available and directs readers to materials from earlier semesters. Jupyter notebooks combine executable code with explanation, making them a practical format for examining computational methods. The repository also points to Persian-language course videos and additional resources. Its public availability establishes access to teaching materials, rather than open admission to the university or the award of academic credit. [s3]

Taken together, these sources illustrate distinct layers of learning: foundational programming and mathematics, an introductory survey of intelligent methods, and more focused machine-learning study. That sequence is an editorial synthesis of the inspected materials, not a nationally mandated pathway. The sources explain what is taught more clearly than whom it reaches. A fuller account of AI education in Iran still requires evidence about institutions outside these examples, access to computing resources, participation, and the assessment of practical competence. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Cybersecurity Education
description: Published Sharif University of Technology courses illustrate cybersecurity teaching through network protection and the security of machine-learning systems. Their outlines combine technical analysis with privacy, measurement ethics, and restrictions on misuse, but do not establish the scale of cybersecurity education across Iran.

seo.title: Cybersecurity Education in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented Iranian cybersecurity teaching examples covering network defense, privacy, machine-learning security, and responsible research.

content.heading: Learning to reason about network risk
content.content:
Sharif University of Technology’s published Advanced Network Security course for Fall 2025 describes protection of modern networks at Internet scale. Its opening topics identify assets, trust boundaries, attacker capabilities, and risks to confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy. In practical terms, students are asked to consider what needs protection, who might threaten it, and which failures matter. [s1]

The outline also addresses what defenders can observe when traffic is encrypted. It distinguishes information available from endpoints, networks, and the Internet’s control systems, alongside privacy constraints. Detection topics include signatures, anomalies, and the consequences of false alarms or missed attacks. Transport-security teaching covers TLS and QUIC, protocols used to protect communications, together with certificate issuance, revocation, and transparency. These are documented syllabus topics; the page does not independently demonstrate that every scheduled activity occurred or that students achieved operational proficiency. [s1]

content.heading: Security of machine-learning systems
content.content:
A separate Sharif course, Security and Privacy in Machine Learning, is also labeled Fall 2025. It examines vulnerabilities during model training and use, together with methods intended to improve robustness and privacy. Its published schedule includes adversarial examples, poisoning, model extraction, and privacy-related topics. These extend cybersecurity teaching beyond conventional network administration to the behavior of learned systems. [s2]

The course explicitly addresses the possibility that the technologies studied could infringe others’ rights. Its policy restricts misuse and requires instructor permission where an activity could be perceived as such. This establishes a stated classroom boundary, rather than evidence about compliance outside the course. It is also an institutional course policy, not a complete account of Iranian law. [s2]

content.title: Two documented areas of cybersecurity teaching

content.summary: The branches identify subjects in two published course outlines. They do not indicate prerequisites, institutional reporting lines, or a national qualification framework.

content.heading: From course descriptions to educational outcomes
content.content:
These examples show why cybersecurity education involves both technical mechanisms and judgments about evidence and permissible activity. The network-security outline includes consent, data minimization, and retention, while the machine-learning course makes responsible use an explicit condition of participation. The interpretation supported here is limited but useful: the published teaching designs recognize privacy and ethics alongside technical analysis. [s1][s2]

They cannot establish a national workforce pipeline, the availability of specialist teaching outside Sharif, or the effectiveness of professional training. Nor does the existence of an advanced course show that a beginner can enroll without prior preparation. A complete account needs broader institutional evidence and independent information about practical assessment, access, and graduate destinations.
